title: Web Platform Lineage Atlas
description: A teaching map of the standards that shaped the modern web: HTML, CSS, ECMAScript, HTTP, browser APIs and WebAssembly. Relationships describe standards evolution or integration, not code inheritance.

curriculumPresets.title: Full web platform atlas
curriculumPresets.description: Explore how document, presentation, scripting, transport and application standards developed together.

curriculumPresets.title: Web development: core foundations
curriculumPresets.description: Trace the current HTML, CSS and ECMAScript branches, then explain why a website relies on separate structure, presentation and behaviour standards.

curriculumPresets.title: Networking: HTTP evolution
curriculumPresets.description: Compare HTTP generations and identify what changed in message handling, multiplexing and transport without treating newer versions as replacements for HTTP semantics.

curriculumPresets.title: Software development: modern web apps
curriculumPresets.description: Focus on DOM, Fetch, Service Workers, WebSocket, WebGPU and WebAssembly when analysing browser application capabilities and constraints.

curriculumPresets.title: Research: standards and compatibility
curriculumPresets.description: Distinguish fixed editions, revised RFCs, modular snapshots and living standards. Use status and source dates when judging whether guidance is current.

nodes.name: Web Platform
nodes.note: The web platform is a coordinated collection of standards, not one technology. Its major strands evolve independently and integrate through browser implementations.
nodes.hook: Ask learners to separate structure, presentation, behaviour, transport and application APIs before tracing their dependencies.

nodes.name: Document and Markup
nodes.note: HTML evolved from early document markup into a living application and document standard.
nodes.hook: Compare a fixed recommendation with a living standard and discuss how each model handles change.

nodes.name: Early HTML
nodes.note: Early HTML established hypertext documents before formal standardisation moved through IETF and W3C processes.
nodes.hook: Identify which modern responsibilities were already present and which were later separated into CSS and APIs.

nodes.name: HTML 2.0
nodes.note: RFC 1866 documented the HTML in common use before November 1995.
nodes.hook: Use the RFC to show that standards often consolidate existing practice rather than invent everything at once.

nodes.name: HTML 3.2
nodes.note: HTML 3.2 was the first W3C HTML Recommendation and captured widely deployed browser features.
nodes.hook: Discuss the tension between implementation-led features and clean standards design.

nodes.name: HTML 4.01
nodes.note: HTML 4.01 refined HTML 4 and strengthened the separation of document structure from presentation.
nodes.hook: Find deprecated presentational features and relate their removal to CSS responsibility.

nodes.name: XHTML 1.0
nodes.note: XHTML 1.0 reformulated the three HTML 4 document types as XML applications.
nodes.hook: Compare strict XML parsing expectations with error-tolerant HTML parsing.

nodes.name: HTML5
nodes.note: HTML5 consolidated modern document semantics and web application capabilities after renewed W3C and WHATWG work.
nodes.hook: Classify HTML5 additions as semantic elements, media features or application support.

nodes.name: HTML Living Standard
nodes.note: WHATWG uses continuous development rather than numbered HTML versions. The standard was current to 31 August 2026 when checked.
nodes.hook: Explain why saying HTML6 is the next normal release would misrepresent the current standards model.

nodes.name: Presentation and Layout
nodes.note: CSS moved presentation out of markup, then shifted from monolithic levels to independently evolving modules and snapshots.
nodes.hook: Relate modular standards development to browser compatibility and progressive enhancement.

nodes.name: CSS Level 1
nodes.note: CSS1 standardised foundational selectors, properties and cascading behaviour.
nodes.hook: Identify which CSS1 concepts remain fundamental in current stylesheets.

nodes.name: CSS Level 2
nodes.note: CSS2 expanded layout, media and positioning capabilities before implementation experience drove revision.
nodes.hook: Use CSS2 to discuss why a published standard may need correction after implementation.

nodes.name: CSS 2.1
nodes.note: CSS 2.1 corrected CSS2 and documented features with interoperable implementation experience.
nodes.hook: Contrast specification completeness with features browsers actually implement consistently.

nodes.name: CSS Modules
nodes.note: CSS beyond Level 2 is developed as modules at different maturity levels rather than one monolithic CSS3 release.
nodes.hook: Challenge the misconception that all CSS3 features share one version or support level.

nodes.name: CSS Grid Layout
nodes.note: Grid is one major CSS module for two-dimensional layout and continues to evolve independently.
nodes.hook: Compare Grid and Flexbox by layout problem rather than treating one as a replacement for the other.

nodes.name: CSS Snapshot 2026
nodes.note: The 2026 snapshot collects the specifications that define the current state of CSS by stability, not browser adoption alone.
nodes.hook: Ask learners why a current snapshot still does not guarantee universal browser support.

nodes.name: Browser Scripting
nodes.note: JavaScript originated in browsers and was standardised as ECMAScript, which now follows annual editions.
nodes.hook: Separate JavaScript implementations, the ECMAScript language specification and browser APIs.

nodes.name: JavaScript
nodes.note: JavaScript first appeared in Netscape Navigator 2.0 and became a principal originating technology for ECMAScript.
nodes.hook: Explain why JavaScript and ECMAScript are related names but not interchangeable in every context.

nodes.name: ECMAScript 1
nodes.note: The first ECMA-262 edition was adopted in June 1997.
nodes.hook: Use standardisation to discuss interoperability between competing browser implementations.

nodes.name: ECMAScript 3
nodes.note: The third edition became a long-lived baseline for pre-modern JavaScript.
nodes.hook: Compare legacy syntax constraints with current language features.

nodes.name: ECMAScript 5.1
nodes.note: ES5.1 consolidated the pre-ES2015 language and aligned with ISO/IEC 16262:2011.
nodes.hook: Identify common code patterns that pre-date classes, modules and arrow functions.

nodes.name: ECMAScript 2015
nodes.note: The sixth edition introduced the year-based naming convention and a major expansion of the language.
nodes.hook: Connect modules, classes, promises and lexical declarations to modern application structure.

nodes.name: ECMAScript 2026
nodes.note: ECMA-262 17th edition defines ECMAScript 2026 and was approved in June 2026.
nodes.hook: Use the current edition to verify language claims rather than relying on undated JavaScript tutorials.

nodes.name: Web Transport
nodes.note: HTTP versions share semantics but use different message framing and transport approaches.
nodes.hook: Prevent learners from reducing HTTP evolution to a simple speed-version ladder.

nodes.name: HTTP/0.9
nodes.note: The earliest HTTP form was a minimal request and response protocol for hypertext transfer.
nodes.hook: Compare its limited exchange with the metadata and methods expected today.

nodes.name: HTTP/1.0
nodes.note: HTTP/1.0 was documented in RFC 1945 as internet use expanded beyond the earliest protocol.
nodes.hook: Trace why headers, status codes and content types became necessary.

nodes.name: HTTP/1.1
nodes.note: HTTP/1.1 remains current, with its message syntax and connection management revised in RFC 9112 in 2022.
nodes.hook: Explain why HTTP/1.1 remains relevant even when HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 are available.

nodes.name: HTTP/2
nodes.note: HTTP/2 uses binary framing and multiplexed streams while retaining HTTP semantics.
nodes.hook: Model how multiplexing differs from opening independent sequential requests.

nodes.name: HTTP/3
nodes.note: HTTP/3 maps HTTP semantics over QUIC rather than TCP.
nodes.hook: Separate application semantics from the transport used to carry them.

nodes.name: WebSocket
nodes.note: WebSocket begins with an HTTP upgrade handshake and then provides full-duplex messaging under its own protocol.
nodes.hook: Choose between request-response, server-sent updates and bidirectional messaging for sample applications.

nodes.name: Browser APIs
nodes.note: Browser APIs connect documents, scripting, networking, storage, background work and hardware capabilities.
nodes.hook: Ask which capabilities belong to ECMAScript itself and which come from the host browser.

nodes.name: DOM Level 1
nodes.note: DOM Level 1 standardised a platform-neutral way to represent and manipulate document structure.
nodes.hook: Connect the document tree model to selectors, events and scripted updates.

nodes.name: DOM Level 2
nodes.note: DOM Level 2 extended the model across areas including events, style and traversal.
nodes.hook: Relate modular API growth to the later living-standard model.

nodes.name: DOM Living Standard
nodes.note: The WHATWG DOM Standard continuously defines the core node, event and mutation model used by other web standards.
nodes.hook: Trace one DOM method from specification concept to a browser console example.

nodes.name: XMLHttpRequest
nodes.note: XMLHttpRequest standardised scripted network requests that had already enabled early asynchronous web applications.
nodes.hook: Compare callback-oriented XHR with promise-oriented Fetch code.

nodes.name: Fetch Standard
nodes.note: Fetch unifies network fetching concepts used across browsers, including requests, responses, CORS and service worker integration.
nodes.hook: Follow a request through URL parsing, policy checks, HTTP and response handling.

nodes.name: Service Workers
nodes.note: Service workers receive events outside a page context and can intercept fetches to support offline and background behaviour.
nodes.hook: Design a caching strategy and identify when stale data becomes a risk.

nodes.name: WebGPU
nodes.note: WebGPU exposes modern GPU rendering and compute capabilities through a web standard.
nodes.hook: Compare the security and portability constraints of browser GPU access with native graphics APIs.

nodes.name: Portable Binary Runtime
nodes.note: WebAssembly provides a portable low-level code format that integrates with JavaScript and browser APIs rather than replacing them.
nodes.hook: Challenge the misconception that WebAssembly is simply a new JavaScript version.

nodes.name: WebAssembly 1.0
nodes.note: The first core WebAssembly recommendation established the portable stack-machine format.
nodes.hook: Map source language, compiler, Wasm module and browser runtime as separate stages.

nodes.name: WebAssembly 2.0
nodes.note: WebAssembly 2.0 expanded the core standard before the current 3.0 release line.
nodes.hook: Use versioned binary formats to discuss backwards compatibility and feature detection.

nodes.name: WebAssembly 3.0
nodes.note: The current W3C core specification page describes release 3.0, checked in September 2026.
nodes.hook: Verify runtime support separately from the publication date of a standard.
